deck: This week sees new ventures in satellite ownership and budget boosts for space resilience.

stories.head: Starlink veterans launch new megaconstellation venture
stories.body: A group of former SpaceX engineers has founded a startup aimed at expanding megaconstellation ownership for governments and corporations. The venture's goal is to democratize access to satellite services, which could reshape the competitive landscape that SpaceX has dominated. If successful, this could mean a more fragmented market, but one that may also offer better service diversity.
stories.soWhat: If the startup gains traction, expect SpaceX to feel the heat—competition in the satellite space is about to get more interesting.

stories.head: Rocket Lab secures NASA award for three launches
stories.body: NASA has awarded Rocket Lab three Electron launches for science missions slated for 2027, valued at an undisclosed amount but a clear win for the company. This award comes after a lengthy selection process, raising eyebrows about NASA's timeline for mission planning. Rocket Lab’s ability to deliver on these launches will be closely watched as it attempts to solidify its role in the science payload market.
stories.soWhat: NASA's slow decision-making might just be Rocket Lab's gain; it’s a reminder that patience can occasionally pay off in government contracts.

stories.head: True Anomaly raises $190M Series C amid defense pull
stories.body: True Anomaly has successfully raised $190 million in a Series C round, bringing its valuation to $1.6 billion. The funding underscores the growing interest in co-orbital security and space domain awareness, with the Department of Defense increasingly pulling in private sector capabilities. As defense budgets tighten, this capital influx indicates a market shift towards more private-public partnerships.
stories.soWhat: True Anomaly's funding is a sign that the defense sector is serious about space—if you’re not thinking co-orbital, you might be missing the boat.

talent.statLabel: Job orders YoY · plus 2 starters per head, an 8-year first
talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.
